### Introduction

Every morning, millions of people reach for a moisturizer, a foundation, a mascara, a lip gloss, and other cosmetics before 8am. We trust these products completely. They smell good, they feel good, and they come in beautiful packaging. But buried inside many of those sleek bottles and colorful palettes are ingredients that scientists and public health researchers have flagged as potentially harmful.

I had no idea how many of my own products appeared on the California Safe Cosmetics Program (CSCP) list when I first started looking into this. The CSCP is a program run by the California Department of Public Health that requires cosmetic companies selling in California state to report any products containing chemicals linked to cancer, birth defects or reproductive harm. The data is from year 2009 to 2020, and includes product names, brands, company names, and the specific chemicals of concern.

I wanted to turn this data into something anyone could read and learn from. So, I built an infographic around following four questions:

**Which harmful chemicals show up most often across cosmetic products?**

**Which companies have the largest number of reported products?**

**Which luxury brands expose consumers to the widest variety of harmful chemicals?**

**Which popular brands has less harmful chemicals?**

You can [explore the full dataset here](https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/chemicals-in-cosmetics-d55bf).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Infographic

![The chemistry of beauty: An infographic exploring harmful chemicals in cosmetic products reported to the California Safe Cosmetics Program between 2009 and 2020.](infographic_final.png)

My final infographic is made up of four visualizations, all built in R using `{ggplot2}` and assembled in Affinity designer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Design Process

### 1. Graphic Form

I used three chart types across the infographic, each chosen for a specific reason.

The **card layout** for the top 5 chemicals uses `geom_tile()` for the card backgrounds and a Font Awesome warning icon on each card. I wanted the ranking to feel intuitive, the kind of list you read in seconds without thinking about axes or scale. A bar chart would have been more conventional but less visually engaging for a general audience.

The **horizontal bar chart** for the top 10 companies uses `coord_flip()` because company names are long and a vertical axis makes them hard to read. Each bar gets a direct label so it will be easy to read the axis text.

The **packed bubble chart** for brand chemical diversity uses `circleProgressiveLayout()` from the `{packcircles}` package. Bubble size reflects the number of unique harmful chemical types per brand. Bubble charts feel less rigid than bar charts and invite you to look around the whole canvas, which felt right for a question about brands you recognize.

The **luxury brand bubble chart** uses the same approach, but bubble size reflects product count instead of chemical diversity, so you can compare how many products each brand has reported alongside how many chemical types they use.

### 2. Text (Titles, Labels, Annotations)

Every chart has a direct title that states the question, not a generic description. I removed all axis titles where the labels already made the meaning obvious. Each bubble in the brand charts is labeled with both the brand name and a count line so the size comparison is always backed up by numbers.

The subtitle on the brand bubble chart calls out Palladio by name because naming a specific brand makes the finding feel real in a way that an abstract ranking does not.

### 3. Themes

All charts use `theme_void()` or `theme_minimal()` as the base, with the grid removed entirely. I kept the layout clean because the data is already visually busy enough. White backgrounds are used throughout to keep things readable and light.

### 4. Colors

I built a custom palette called **Velvet Dawn**: muted roses, warm sands, dusty wines, slate indigo, dusty brick red, and a pale ivory. The palette is inspired by the cosmetics world, soft and warm rather than clinical or alarming.

``` r
palette <- c(
  "rose"   = "#D8A7B1",  # Rose Dust
  "sand"   = "#E6C9A8",  # Warm Sand
  "plum"   = "#8E6A7A",  # Muted Plum
  "almond" = "#F5E6D8",  # Pale Almond
  "wine"   = "#9B4A5A",  # Dusty Wine
  "sky"    = "#A8BED1",  # Hazy Sky
  "olive"  = "#9DA87A",  # Muted Olive
  "butter" = "#EDD9A3",  # Pale Butter
  "indigo" = "#7B7DB5",  # Slate Indigo
  "brick"  = "#B85C5C"   # Dusty Brick Red
)
```

The colors are not perfectly colorblind friendly in every combination, but I was careful to never rely on color alone to carry a key message. Every important finding is also encoded through position, labels, or text.

### 5. Typography

I used two fonts throughout:

-   **EB Garamond** for titles and captions, elegant and editorial
-   **Jost** for data labels, counts, and annotations, clean and geometric

Both fonts were loaded using `font_add_google()` from `{sysfonts}` and activated with `showtext_auto()`. I also used **Noteworthy** inside Affinity Designer for decorative text elements in the infographic layout.

### 6. General Design

The four panels are ordered deliberately. You start with what chemicals are showing up, move to which companies are responsible, then look at brand-level chemical diversity, and end with the luxury brand comparison. Each panel raises the next question naturally.

I filtered the brand bubble chart to brands with at least 30 products to avoid small brands ranking high by coincidence. This filter is stated in the subtitle so readers understand why some brands they expected are not there.

### 7. Contextualizing the Data

The infographic opens with a plain statement of the problem: cosmetics in the U.S. do not need FDA approval before they are sold, and companies decide what is safe. That framing is there so readers understand why this data matters before they look at any chart.

The definition of harmful chemicals is also stated directly inside the infographic: ingredients linked to cancer, birth defects, or reproductive harm, required by California law to be reported.

### 8. Primary message

The central message is that harmful chemicals are widespread in cosmetics across all price points, from drugstore brands to luxury houses. The infographic is designed so that message is visible even if a reader only looks at the bubble charts without reading the text.

The biggest surprise in the data, Palladio leading with 12 distinct harmful chemical types, is called out by name in the subtitle of the brand bubble chart. That specificity makes the finding land harder than an abstract ranking would.

### 9. Accessibility

Font sizes are large enough to read without zooming. Every key finding is readable through labels and annotations, not just visual encoding. The bubble charts label each circle with explicit counts so size comparisons are always backed up by numbers.

Alt text is provided for the infographic image above.

### 10. DEI Lens

The data covers products reported to the CSCP between 2009 and 2020. It reflects what companies chose to report, not a complete picture of every harmful ingredient in every product on the market. That limitation is worth naming: the dataset captures reported chemicals, and some companies may have underreported.

The infographic focuses on consumer exposure rather than regulatory compliance, because the people most affected by this data are everyday shoppers, not regulators.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Reflections

The finding that surprised me most was Palladio. I expected the top of the brand chart to be dominated by large, well-known brands. Instead, a niche mineral makeup brand most people have never heard of leads with 12 distinct harmful chemical types across just 96 products.

The luxury brand chart was also revealing. Dior leads the group with 6 chemical types and 367 products, which is more than Chanel, Givenchy, or Estee Lauder. Price is clearly not a reliable signal of chemical safety.

The hardest part of this project was the brand name cleaning. The raw dataset has 2,573 unique brand name entries for what is actually a much smaller set of real brands. "Parfums Chrisitian Dior", "Parfums Christain Dior", and "Parfums Christian Dior" are three separate entries for the same brand, with three different typos. Collapsing those variants using `str_detect()` inside `case_when()` took more time than any single visualization.

## Explore the Code

All visualizations were built in R using `{ggplot2}`, `{packcircles}`, `{ggtext}`, `{showtext}`, and `{glue}`. The full code is available in the expandable chunk below.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(janitor)
library(scales)
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)
library(showtext)
library(sysfonts)
library(glue)
library(packcircles)
library(ggtext)
library(here)
```

```{r}
#| label: import-fonts
#| echo: true

font_add_google(name = "Jost",       family = "jost")
font_add_google(name = "EB Garamond", family = "eb-garamond")
font_add(family = "fa-brands",
         regular = here::here("fonts", "Font Awesome 7 Brands-Regular-400.otf"))
font_add(family = "fa-solid",
         regular = here::here("fonts", "Font Awesome 7 Free-Solid-900.otf"))

showtext_auto()
showtext_opts(dpi = 300)
```

```{r}
#| label: read-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false

cscp_data <- read_csv(here::here("data", "cscpopendata.csv")) %>%
  clean_names()
```

```{r}
#| label: data-cleaning
#| echo: true

cscp_clean <- cscp_data %>%
  mutate(
    initial_date_reported     = mdy(initial_date_reported),
    most_recent_date_reported = mdy(most_recent_date_reported),
    discontinued_date         = mdy(discontinued_date),
    chemical_created_at       = mdy(chemical_created_at),
    chemical_updated_at       = mdy(chemical_updated_at),
    chemical_date_removed     = mdy(chemical_date_removed)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    report_year  = year(initial_date_reported),
    report_month = month(initial_date_reported, label = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(
    c(primary_category, sub_category, chemical_name, company_name, brand_name),
    str_trim
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(chemical_name))
```
